text.text:
### Prerequisites

In this text, we will keep exploring the idea of equality: we will compare how different cultures understand the "world". For a more detailed understanding, we recommend studying the earlier comparison texts in the "First Steps" section (<htcite0>).

### Introduction

In the previous text, we learned that calendars, in general, count the number of days that pass from a starting point. Although they share the same idea, different cultures created calendars in different ways (<htcite0>).

This fact, related to time, leads us to a reflection:

Reflection 1: Is it only about time?

If people in different cultures had different understandings of how time is counted, is it also possible that they had different understandings of other things, such as the idea of the world?

### A local view

To better understand how the "world" was conceived in ancient times, we need to dive into the period people lived in and how they described their world — this way we avoid misleading generalizations.

#### A Mesoamerican case

In <htdate0>, the city of Copan was conquered by the same general who conquered Tikal: Sihyaj K’ahk’, who had ties to Teotihuacan, located in central Mexico (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). Given this fact, we can conclude that they had at least heard of the region.

On the other hand, when we look at the inscription of Stela A (Figure 1), written in the times of Waxaklajuun Ubaah K’awiil — also known as 18 Rabbit — and made before <htdate1>, the year of his death (<htcite2>), we see that the conquerors are not mentioned in its description. At that time, only four great urban centers are mentioned — Copan, Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque — representing the cardinal points (<htcite3>; <htcite4>).
Figure 1: Stela A at the Site Museum of Copán, with a mention of the cities of Copán, Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque, in that order (). Photo taken on , during a visit to the site.

source.text: Instituto Hondureño de Antropologia e Historia

text.imgdesc: In this image, there is a hieroglyphic text arranged in two columns.

text.text: The absence of any mention of cities outside the Maya environment leads us to a reflection:

Reflection 2: A new horizon

At that time, the world of Copán no longer had Teotihuacan on the horizon, because the city had lost the dominance it once had.

Would it make sense for them to mention it?

Does the local world turn what exists around it into something non-existent?

From this reflection, we can conclude that the relevance of the four great centers is highlighted by their mention. That relevance, however, does not rule out the existence of cities earlier than or contemporary to them.

### The Roman world

Since Stela A (Figure 1) was written after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, in <htdate0> (<htcite0>), for a better comparison with texts from the Roman Empire, we will use another city that was contemporary to it: Teotihuacan (Figure 2).
Figure 2: General view of Teotihuacan. Photo taken on , during a visit to the site.
text.imgdesc: General view of the city of Teotihuacan. Several talud-tablero structures can be seen, and in the background two pyramid-like structures, which represent sacred mountains.

text.text:
#### The dimensions of Teotihuacan

The victory of Teotihuacan over Tikal (Guatemala) and the influence that extended to Copan (Honduras) were no accident.

Archaeological excavations show that the city was inhabited between <htdate0> and <htdate1>. During its apogee (<htdate2> - <htdate3>), Teotihuacan came to have 100,000 inhabitants, making it the sixth largest city in the world, behind cities such as Rome, Constantinople and Alexandria (<htcite0>).

Reflection 3: As big as you

Given the importance Teotihuacan had in its time, and the fact that it was contemporary to the Roman Empire, can we conclude that Rome would have made some kind of mention of the city?

#### The Roman view

When we examine speech 26 by Aelius Aristides, addressed to Rome in the second century of the Gregorian calendar, we find great advances regarding the "inhabited world". Below, we highlight some of the places mentioned — the numbers indicate the paragraphs of the speech (<htcite0>):
- **6**: Argos, present-day Greece
- **8**: "Italy... as far as the Strait of Otranto", the strait between Italy and Albania (<htcite1>).
- **9**: Athens and Laconia, both in Greece.
- **10**: There is a mention of Asia, Africa and Europe without stating the known limits of the continents. Chelidonian and Cyanean are also mentioned as the limit of the empire in Anatolia, present-day Turkey.
- **12**: India and Arabia are mentioned, along with Greek regions such as Naxos, in Sicily (<htcite2>), Cythnos and Athens. Finally, farms in Egypt and Sicily and part of Africa classified as civilized are mentioned.
- **13**: The Roman understanding of the world is evident in this passage of the speech: "..and as Hesiod mentioned about the end of the Ocean, there is a common channel where all waters have a single origin and destination; therefore there is a common channel to Rome and all gather here."
- **15**: A mention of the Persian Empire and its relation to the Hellenes, the Greeks.
- **16**: Mentions of the Atlantics and the Mediterranean Sea.
- **17**: Further mentions of regions such as Ionia, the coast of Greece (<htcite3>), and Lydia in Turkey. Beyond these regions, we also note a mention of a region beyond the Euphrates.
- **18**: Continuing with regions of Mesopotamia and beyond, we see references to Emperor Cyrus, as well as Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana, the latter two in present-day Iran (<htcite4>; <htcite5>).
- **22 and 23**: Further mentions of the Persian Empire.
- **24 - 27**: Mentions of Alexander and his conquests. In one mention it is said that he "advanced over most of the land". At the end, it mentions that the Macedonian empire was divided with his death.
- **28**: When mentioning the reach of the empire's expansion, he mentions the Red Sea, the cataracts of the Nile and the Sea of Azov. Another point worth highlighting in his speech is the fact that some writers "did not believe the ocean existed".
- **31**: Again there is a mention of a "civilized world".
- **36**: Mention of Caria and Phrygia, in present-day Turkey (<htcite6>), and of Egypt.
- **42 - 59**: Description of the Hellenic states.
- **60**: There is a description of the Roman Empire we wish to highlight: "Neither the sea nor the continent that lies between them are barriers to citizenship, nor do Asia and Europe receive different treatment here. In his empire, all paths are open to all".
- **63**: Still about the people around the Roman world, we note the mention: "For the categories by which you now divide the world are not Greeks and barbarians — and the distinction you made is not absurd, since you present them with a citizenship, so to speak, more numerous than the whole Hellenic race. The division you adopted in its place is between Romans and non-Romans. To such a length have you extended the name of your city."
- **73 - 74**: Mentions of Greeks and Egyptians.
- **82**: The region of Aethiopia, located in the south of Egypt, is mentioned alongside Phasis, a region near the Black Sea.
- **85 - 86**: We have mentions of the Persians and the Egyptians.
- **91**: A mention of the process of enslavement: "The Macedonians knew slavery under the Persians; the Persians, under the Medes; the Medes, under the Assyrians; but, since men have news of you, all have known you as rulers."
- **101**: We recover a phrase from Homer: "Common land for all".

Despite the use of the word "Earth" and also of "world", an analysis of the places mentioned in the speech shows no knowledge associated with the peoples living in America (*Abya Yala*).

Furthermore, we stress that Aelius Aristides himself mentions that some writers did not know the ocean.
Considering that Aelius Aristides had much greater knowledge than the general population of the Roman Empire, let us make a new reflection:

Reflection 4: If the one who knows, does not know. The one who does not know...

Aelius Aristides mentions an earth and a world that are not the earth and the world we know today. Even so, his description of the Roman world is quite broad.

If he, Aelius Aristides, with all the studies and information he had, did not know the world as we know it, could anyone inside the empire, without his knowledge, have any idea of the world as we know it today?

Assuming that for some reason you conclude the answer is yes, what archaeological evidence would you use to prove it?

### A Babylonian view

As human knowledge grows over time, we can expect that, the further back we go in time, we will find an even more restricted view of what the world was.

A good example of this appears when we analyze the earliest map we know of, made in Babylon (Figure 4).
Figure 4: Map of the "world" © Trustees of the British Museum (). Shared under the license Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
text.imgdesc: In this figure, we have a clay tablet with inscriptions. On it, there is a large central circle, with triangles on its outer part.

text.text: This map from Babylon shows that, in their understanding, the world was limited to nearby lands — with no mention of other continents or seas (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). Quite different from what we understand today as the planet Earth (<htcite2>; <htcite3>).

source.text: Hu, X., Shum, C.K. & Bevis, M

text.text: To make the regions represented by the Babylonian map more evident, compared to what we know of our current world, we follow Dr. Irving Finkel’s explanation (<htcite0>) and overlay the Babylonian map on the current world map (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Babylonian world map © Trustees of the British Museum () superimposed on the current world map © Mapswire (). Shared under the license Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
text.imgdesc: In this image, one can see that the ancient Babylonian map occupies an extremely small area compared to the world we know today.

text.text:
### Conclusion

In this text, we saw world descriptions from three distinct peoples (Maya, Romans and Babylonians). None of the descriptions we analyzed reflects what we know about our current world, even though, in the times of the Roman Empire, the description used words such as "earth" and "world".

Simply saying that they were wrong can lead us into an error. What we saw in this text actually shows that words change meaning over time: we must not only read a text, but also study the words and the era in which the authors lived, in order to truly understand what they meant in their texts.

exercise_v2.question: Has humanity always understood the Earth with its current shape and described it exactly as we know it today?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Our knowledge of the Earth, and of nature as a whole, has grown over time. Ancient texts, maps and stelae show that descriptions of places did not necessarily reflect the world we know today, even though some peoples called the region they knew the world.

exercise_v2.question: In the speech we studied about the Roman Empire, is it clear that the Romans knew of Teotihuacan?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Nowhere in the text we studied is there any mention of the peoples living in America (Abya Yala). Furthermore, there is no archaeological finding that would allow us to suppose that these peoples had come into contact with one another.
